# Documentation Rules

- Treat `readme.txt` as a WordPress.org plugin readme using WordPress readme syntax, not generic plain text or GitHub Markdown.
- Preserve the existing WordPress readme section markers and formatting conventions in `readme.txt`.
- `README.md` stays a short GitHub pointer to the WordPress.org plugin page. Do not copy the readme or changelog into it.
- Treat `changelog.md` as the full changelog. `readme.txt` repeats the unreleased section when one exists, otherwise the latest release, then the existing `### Full Changelog` link to `changelog.md`.
- The version sections already in those files are released. Do not add bullets under them. Ask for the next version before starting a section.
- Preserve changelog bullets: a category label, a colon, then the sentence. Use the labels already in the file, such as `Added`, `Fixed`, `Changed`, `Improved`, `Removed`, `Security`, `Updated`, and `Upgrade`.
- Keep version headings in the form already used, such as `= 2.2.0 =`, in both `changelog.md` and `readme.txt`. Use the real version, not this sample.
- Nested detail stays a tab-indented bullet under the item it explains.
- When copying content from code, such as docblocks, comments, or commit notes, into `changelog.md`, `readme.txt`, or other user-facing docs, preserve the essence verbatim. Only minor prose tweaks for readability are allowed. Do not add details that are not present in the source.
- A symbol introduced in the unreleased version gets one changelog introduction. Do not add a later entry for edits made to it before release.
- When mentioning a public function, constant, hook, or option, use the fully qualified name, for example `Pro_Mime_Types\get_allowed_mime_types_settings()` or `pmt_supported_mime_types`.
